docs.title: Post-processing tools and helper models for G4X-data
docs.text: With G4X-helpers we provide an open-source toolkit for common post-processing tasks — such as applying custom segmentations or adding your own labels to the G4X-viewer. You can access its core features from the command-line interface (CLI) and additionally import it as a standalone Python package to interact with your data.

docs.title: Reference documentation for G4X-data files
docs.text: The G4X produces multi-modal output containing tables, images, arrays and annotated matrices for single-cell analysis. The files found in the output directory are compatible with popular Python libraries from the scverse ecosystem, like scanpy, rapids-singlecell, squidpy, and spatial-data, and, if you prefer working in R, can be easily imported into Seurat.

docs.title: G4X-data import
docs.text:
The multi-modal output of the G4X spatial sequencer comprises images, tables and annotated data matrices, which allow deep exploration of your sample. The single_cell_data folder contains both per-cell counts aggregated from the segmentation and processed analysis outputs. Choose an input based on whether you want to start a new analysis or continue the provided analysis.

Goal Input Contents Start a new analysis with your own filtering and normalization cell_by_gene.csv.gz and cell_metadata.csv.gz Raw transcript counts for the segmented cells, including control probes when present, and associated cell metadata. Continue the provided analysis sc_processed.h5ad Cells and genes retained after filtering, processed RNA values, and analysis results such as PCA, UMAP, and clustering when processing succeeds.

The processed AnnData can contain fewer cells and genes than the CSV tables. Its .obs metadata describe only the retained cells and can include additional analysis annotations.

docs.title: Below we illustrate data import strategies for Python and R users:
if you are working in Python
docs.text:
Some excellent tools are:

  • scanpy: full-featured single-cell analysis suite
  • rapids-singlecell: expands scanpy with GPU-support
  • squidpy: functionality for the analysis of spatial data
  • spatial-data: analysis and management of spatial data (requires data conversion)

All of these tools accept, or incorporate anndata objects as the basic representation of your single-cell data. The first two methods below load the provided processed AnnData; the third builds a new object from raw counts. These workflows differ in their cell/gene selection, RNA values, and available annotations.

docs.title: Understanding the processed AnnData
docs.text:
Processing filters cells using quality measures such as cell area, transcript counts, detected genes, control-probe percentage, and available nuclear stain measurements. Gene filtering retains targeting genes with sufficient cell coverage. The retained counts are then normalized by total counts per cell and transformed with log1p.

When preprocessing completes, adata.X contains these normalized, log-transformed RNA values. adata.layers["counts"] preserves the raw counts for the same retained cells and genes. This layer does not restore cells, genes, or control probes removed during filtering; use the CSV count matrix when you need those values. Avoid treating adata.X as raw counts or repeating normalization on it unintentionally.

If processing stops before normalization, the saved object may lack the counts layer and some analysis results. Check the available layers and annotations before continuing an analysis.

For multiomics data, adata.obsm["protein"] contains the per-cell mean protein intensities, with rows aligned to adata.obs_names. The corresponding column names, in order, are stored in adata.uns["protein_names"]. Protein intensities are separate from the RNA matrix in adata.X:

# After loading the processed AnnData using either method below:
protein_values = adata.obsm["protein"]
protein_names = adata.uns["protein_names"]

The CSV import example below loads RNA and cell metadata only. To include protein measurements in a new analysis, also load cell_by_protein.csv.gz and align its rows by cell_id.

docs.title: 1. G4X-helpers
docs.text:
If you have G4X-helpers v4 installed, you can use the G4Xsample() class to access the anndata of your sample via the load_adata() method.

import g4x_helpers as g4x

run_base = '/path/to/g4x_data/sample_x1'

sample = g4x.G4Xsample(run_base)
adata = sample.load_adata(remove_nontargeting=False, load_clustering=False)

Note: load_adata() options

load_adata() provides options that control which data are returned. processed: bool (default=True) remove_nontargeting: bool (default=False) load_clustering: bool (default=False)

docs.title: 2. scanpy
docs.text:
You can load the saved processed object directly by pointing scanpy's read_h5ad() function to sc_processed.h5ad in your G4X-data directory. This preserves the annotations stored in the file; the Helpers example above uses load_clustering=False and omits Leiden columns from .obs.

from pathlib import Path
import scanpy as sc

run_base = Path('/path/to/g4x_data/sample_x1')
ad_file = run_base / 'single_cell_data' / 'sc_processed.h5ad'

adata = sc.read_h5ad(ad_file)

Note

If you have G4X-helpers installed, then scanpy will be available as one of its dependencies. If not, please refer to the scanpy documentation for installation guides.

docs.title: 3. building from raw data
docs.text:
With G4X-helpers, use G4Xsample.load_adata(processed=False) to build a new, unfiltered AnnData from the per-cell count and metadata tables and transcript manifest, rather than loading sc_processed.h5ad:

import g4x_helpers as g4x

sample = g4x.G4Xsample('/path/to/g4x_data/sample_x1')
adata = sample.load_adata(processed=False)

This keeps raw RNA counts in .X, including control probes when present, and adds gene annotations and calculated QC metrics. It also includes protein intensities when available. It does not filter cells or genes, normalize or log-transform counts, or compute PCA, UMAP, or clustering. By default, remove_nontargeting=False and load_clustering=False.

Alternatively, to start a new RNA analysis without G4X-helpers, read the raw counts and cell metadata directly into an anndata object. Its .X contains raw counts, including control probes when present. The manual example below does not apply filtering or normalization, or load the provided clustering, embeddings, gene metadata, or protein matrix.

from pathlib import Path
import anndata as ad
import pandas as pd
from scipy import sparse

run_base = Path('/path/to/g4x_data/sample_x1')

txcounts_path = run_base / 'single_cell_data' / 'cell_by_gene.csv.gz'
metadata_path = run_base / 'single_cell_data' / 'cell_metadata.csv.gz'

counts = pd.read_csv(txcounts_path, index_col='cell_id')
X = sparse.csr_matrix(counts.values)

metadata = pd.read_csv(metadata_path, index_col='cell_id')

adata = ad.AnnData(X=X, obs=metadata)
adata.var_names = counts.columns

Note

If you have G4X-helpers installed, then anndata, pandas and scipy will be available as dependencies.

docs.title: if you are working in R
docs.text:
The most feature rich package for single-cell analysis in R is:

  • Seurat: full-featured single-cell analysis suite with spatial analysis capabilities

To work with your data in Seurat, it needs to be loaded into a SeuratObject, which is an annotated data structure. This example starts from the raw RNA count matrix and cell metadata, so you can apply your own filtering and normalization in Seurat. It does not reproduce the provided processed AnnData analysis or load protein measurements.

library('Seurat')

run_base = c('/path/to/g4x_data/sample_x1')

txcounts_path = file.path(run_base, "single_cell_data/cell_by_gene.csv.gz")
metadata_path = file.path(run_base, "single_cell_data/cell_metadata.csv.gz")

counts <- read.csv(txcounts_path, row.names = 1) 
counts <- t(counts) # transpose to match Seurat input

metadata <- read.csv(metadata_path, row.names = 1) 

sobj <- CreateSeuratObject(counts = counts, meta.data = metadata)

docs.title: Output file reference
docs.text:
This page provides a comprehensive reference for all output files generated by the G4X platform. It describes the contents of each directory and file type. Special notes are included for files specific to multiomics runs. The documentation also highlights file compatibility with the G4X-viewer and provides detailed column descriptions for key tables.

This symbol indicates that these files are only available in multiomics runs.

docs.title: Table field availability
docs.text:
Where a table lists field availability:

  • Required means the field is required by the current G4X-helpers table validator. This describes column presence, not a guarantee that every value is non-null.
  • Conditional means the field is produced at a particular processing stage or for a particular assay. Check the stated condition before using it.
  • Optional means consumers should allow the field to be absent; its presence may depend on the segmentation, producer, or software version.

Panel-specific gene/protein columns and analysis-specific cluster annotations can vary between samples. The RNA and single-cell references describe these variable columns explicitly. CSV types describe the meaning of the values rather than a fixed on-disk dtype; readers may infer different numeric types, and cell identifiers may be read as strings or integers.

docs.title: g4x-viewer.zarr
docs.text:
The g4x-viewer.zarr directory is a G4X-viewer compatible Zarr store. It contains optimized representations of images, cell metadata, cell polygons, transcript locations, and summary content for interactive visualization.

These files are intended for visual exploration with the G4X-viewer, not as the primary source for quantitative analysis. For analysis workflows, use the raw images, transcript tables, masks, and single_cell_data files documented in this section.

docs.title: images
docs.text: Zarr groups containing multiscale image pyramids for the multiplex image stack and fH&E image. The multiplex image includes nuclear and cytoplasmic stain channels, plus protein channels in multiomics runs.

docs.title: cells
docs.text: Zarr groups containing segmentation-specific cell metadata, polygon vertices, expression matrix indices, protein intensities, UMAP coordinates, and cluster labels. The default segmentation group is g4x_default_segmentation.

docs.title: transcripts
docs.text: Tiled Zarr groups containing viewer-ready transcript coordinates, cell assignments, and gene identifiers.

docs.title: misc
docs.text:
Additional viewer assets, including summary.html when a sample summary report is available.

metadata updates

The G4X-helpers viewer commands can export and import metadata for images, cells, and transcripts in an existing g4x-viewer.zarr store.

docs.title: h_and_e.ome.tiff
docs.text: Raw, full-sized fH&E image.

docs.title: nuclear.ome.tiff
docs.text: Raw, full-sized nuclear stain image.

docs.title: cytoplasmic.ome.tiff
docs.text: Raw, full-sized cytoplasmic stain image.

docs.title: thumbs/{image}_thumbnail.png
docs.text:
Reduced size and compressed thumbnail of each image for easy viewing in standard applications. These files are not suitable for quantitative analysis.

segmentation input

The OME-TIFF images in this folder are suitable inputs for custom segmentation workflows. For more information, see segment data.

docs.title: transcript_core_metrics.csv
docs.text: CSV file containing a set of core metrics for the sample including total transcripts, total area, number of cells and more.

docs.title: protein_core_metrics.csv
docs.text: CSV file containing core protein metrics for the sample, such as signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), background intensity, and Fisher's exact test scores. Fisher scores assess the co-occurrence of each protein signal with its corresponding transcripts (<protein>_fisher_score) and with a random background set (<protein>_fisher_background_score). If no protein-gene pairs are present, the value is unavailable; if the score cannot be computed, the entry is NaN.

docs.title: per_area_metrics.csv
docs.text: CSV file containing a set of metrics for 100 µm2 bins across the sample. Values included area identifiers x/y_bin, area coordinates x/y_bin_min_pixel_coordinate, and total number of transcripts and number of cells for each area.

docs.title: protein
docs.text: This folder is only present in multiomics runs

docs.title: {protein}.ome.tiff
docs.text: Raw, full-sized protein detection image for {protein}. The values in the cell_metadata and cell_by_protein tables are derived by applying cell segmentation masks over these protein images.

docs.title: thumbs/{protein}_thumbnail.png
docs.text: Reduced size and compressed thumbnail of each protein image for easy viewing in standard applications. These files are not suitable for quantitative analysis.

docs.title: raw_features.parquet
docs.text:
Parquet file containing raw transcript feature information pre-demultiplexing. It lists sequence, coordinates and quality scores of all detected features. This file is required for the redemux feature of G4X-helpers.

column type description TXUID str Unique identifier for the transcript sequence str Detected barcode sequence before demultiplexing x_pixel_coordinate float The x-coordinate for the transcript y_pixel_coordinate float The y-coordinate for the transcript z_level int Z layer of identified transcript confidence_score float Mean quality score for the transcript

docs.title: transcript_table.csv.gz
docs.text:
CSV file listing all successfully demultiplexed transcript features. Includes transcript coordinates, quality score, and gene identifier. cell_id is added when transcripts are assigned to cells (will be absent after redemux with --no-downstream). The values in the cell_by_gene table are derived by applying cell segmentation masks over these transcripts.

column type description TXUID str Unique identifier for the transcript confidence_score float Mean quality score for the transcript x_pixel_coordinate float The x coordinate for the transcript y_pixel_coordinate float The y coordinate for the transcript z_level int Z layer index of the transcript probe_name str Probe identifier used for decoding gene_id str Gene identifier for the decoded probe cell_id int Cell the transcript is assigned to (0 = not assigned)

docs.title: sample.g4x
docs.text: JSON file containing sample and run metadata, including sample identity, instrument information, flow cell position, panel references, software version, and output schema version.

docs.title: samplesheet.csv
docs.text: CSV file containing detailed run information, including operator, experimental design, run parameters, flow cell layout, tissue type, and panels used. Also specifies the position of each tissue section on the flow cell.

docs.title: summary_*.html
docs.text: HTML file which gives a high level overview of the experiment outputs, data quality, and performance for the specific sample.

docs.title: transcript_manifest.csv
docs.text: CSV file containing the transcript probe manifest used to demultiplex detected features. The manifest includes probe identifiers, gene names, panel annotations, and probe type annotations.

docs.title: protein_panel.csv
docs.text: CSV file containing a full list of all targeted proteins in this experiment and the panel type (standard, addon).

docs.title: segmentation_mask.npz
docs.text: Compressed NumPy archive containing segmentation masks. This archive holds two arrays: nuclei (nuclear segmentation) and nuclei_exp (expanded nuclear mask, i.e. whole-cell approximation). Label IDs correspond to the cell_id fields used in single_cell_data.

docs.title: bead_mask.npz
docs.text: Compressed NumPy archive containing a boolean bead mask under the bead_mask key. The mask marks regions where focusing beads were detected and is used to remove signal in those areas.

docs.title: cell_metadata.csv.gz
docs.text:
CSV file containing the metadata associated with each cell, including cell identifiers, cell area, stain intensities, and transcript QC metrics when calculated. Protein intensities are stored separately in cell_by_protein.csv.gz. This can be used to build single-cell analysis objects (Seurat/Scanpy) and perform downstream analyses. For more information, see data import.

name type description cell_id str Unique cell identifier derived from the segmentation mask sample_id str Sample identifier tissue_type str Tissue type from sample metadata block str Tissue block identifier from sample metadata seg_source str Segmentation source used to generate the cell cell_x/y float x/y coordinate of the cell centroid cell_area_um float Area of the expanded cell segmentation in µm2 nuclei_area_um float Area of the nuclear segmentation in µm2 total_counts int Total transcript counts log1p_total_counts float Log number of total transcripts n_genes_by_counts int Number of unique genes detected log1p_n_genes_by_counts float Log number of unique genes detected total_counts_ctrl int Total control probe counts log1p_total_counts_ctrl float Log number of control probe counts pct_counts_ctrl float Percentage of counts assigned to control probes *stain_intensity_mean float Mean intensity for nuclear and cytoplasmic stains <protein>_intensity_mean float Mean intensity for a given protein

docs.title: cell_by_gene.csv.gz
docs.text: CSV file containing the cell x gene matrix. Each entry in the table is the count for a given gene in a given cell. Control probes are included as additional columns when present.

docs.title: clustering_umap.csv.gz
docs.text:
CSV file containing pre-computed cluster annotations and UMAP coordinates for cells retained for analysis.

cell_id, UMAP1, and UMAP2 are required by the current Helpers validator. Cluster annotation columns depend on the analysis; current Helpers defaults are leiden_coarse and leiden_fine. They are not universal required column names.

docs.title: dgex.csv.gz
docs.text:
CSV file containing differential gene expression (DGEx) results for the pre-computed clusters from the clustering_umap table.

All columns below are required by the current Helpers DGEx schema.

column type description gene_id str Gene identifier score float Z-score from Wilcoxon rank-sum test logfoldchange float LogFoldChange for the given cluster compared to all other clusters combined pval float P-value from Wilcoxon rank-sum test pval_adj float Adjusted P-value pct_nz_group float Fraction of cells with non-zero expression in the given cluster (0–1; e.g. 0.933 means 93.3%). pct_nz_reference float Fraction of cells with non-zero expression outside the given cluster (0–1). cluster_id str Leiden cluster identity leiden_res str Name of the clustering annotation used for this result, such as leiden_coarse or leiden_fine; this is not a numeric resolution. Each result refers to a gene and cluster within that annotation.

docs.title: sc_processed.h5ad
docs.text: AnnData file containing filtered and processed RNA data with cell and gene metadata. The retained data is used to call clusters and calculate differential gene expression. Filtering is likely to remove cells and genes present in the raw CSV tables; please refer to data import to learn how to build an unprocessed/raw AnnData object. When preprocessing completes, .X contains RNA values normalized by total counts per cell and transformed with log1p. .layers["counts"] contains raw counts for the same retained cells and genes. PCA, UMAP, and clustering results are included when the corresponding processing steps succeed. Outputs saved after an incomplete processing run may lack some layers or annotations. For multiomics data, .obsm["protein"] stores mean protein intensities for the retained cells, with column names in .uns["protein_names"]. These measurements are separate from the RNA matrix.

docs.title: cell_by_protein.csv.gz
docs.text: CSV file containing cell x protein intensity matrix. Each entry in the table is the average protein intensity for a given protein in a cell. These columns are separate from the stain intensity columns in cell_metadata.csv.gz which is provided for all runs.

docs.title: rna_protein_sc_correlation.csv
docs.text: CSV file containing a square correlation matrix between selected transcript counts and protein intensity means, computed per cell. Useful for quickly checking concordance between RNA and protein markers (e.g. CD4 counts vs CD4_intensity_mean).

docs.title: protein_sc_correlation.csv
docs.text: CSV file containing a protein-by-protein correlation matrix of per-cell intensity means, allowing assessment of protein marker co-expression.

docs.text: G4X Tutorials are a collection of example workflows that demonstrate how to analyze G4X-data using popular Python and R libraries. These tutorials cover a wide range of topics, from basic visualizations to advanced analysis techniques.

docs.title: Plotting Spatial Data on the G4X
docs.text: One of the first things you'll want to do with your spatial data is to visualize your data on a spatial plot. G4X outputs are designed to make this information easy to access and plot in a variety of ways. With the tables and data structures provided, you can create a variety of spatial visualizations using tools like Seurat in R or scanpy in Python.

docs.title: Python Visualization
docs.text: This brief tutorial uses the scanpy library and assume that you have a working installation of it on your local system. If you do not, please see the scanpy installation guide for instructions on how to install it.

docs.title: 1. Import libraries
docs.text:
# Import necessary libraries
import scanpy as sc
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

docs.title: 2. Load your data
docs.text:
# Load your data
adata = sc.read_h5ad('path/to/your/data.h5ad')

docs.title: 3. Extract spatial coordinates into a scanpy obsm layer for scanpy compatibility
docs.text:
# Extract spatial coordinates into obsm layer
adata.obsm['X_spatial_cell'] = adata.obs[['cell_x', 'cell_y']].to_numpy()

Note

In order for scanpy to extract this information for default plotting, you have to put (x, y) coordinate pairs for each cell into the obsm layer and name it something starting with X_. You can do this with any pair of coordinates.

docs.title: 4. Plot the spatial coordinates
docs.text:
# Plot the spatial coordinates
plt.figure(figsize=(10,8))
ax = sc.pl.scatter(adata, basis='spatial_cell', color='log1p_total_counts', show=False)

# Flip the y-axis to match image orientation
ax.invert_yaxis()
plt.show()

Note

Here, we're plotting with the color='log1p_total_counts' to visualize the log total transcript counts per cell, but you can replace this with any other variable in your adata.obs or adata.var that is the correct dimensions (1xncells) to visualize different aspects of your data.

docs.title: 5. Save the plot as a PNG file
docs.text:
# Save the plot as PNG
plt.savefig("spatial_plot.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches='tight')

docs.title: R Visualization
docs.text: This brief tutorial uses the ggplot2 library and assumes that you have a working installation of it on your local system. If you do not, please see the ggplot2 installation guide for instructions on how to install it.

docs.title: 1. Load necessary libraries
docs.text:
# Load necessary libraries
library(ggplot2)

docs.title: 2. Load your data and create a Seurat object
docs.text:
# Load your data and create a Seurat object
run_base = c('/path/to/g4x_output/<sample_id>')
metadata_path = file.path(run_base, "single_cell_data/cell_metadata.csv.gz")
meta <- read.csv(gzfile(metadata_path), row.names = 1)

docs.title: 3. Plot spatial coordinates with ggplot2
docs.text:
# Ensure coordinates are numeric
meta$cell_x <- as.numeric(meta$cell_x)
meta$cell_y <- as.numeric(meta$cell_y)

p <- ggplot(meta, aes(x = cell_x, y = cell_y, color=log1p_total_counts)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_y_reverse() +           # <-- invert Y
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "cell_x", y = "cell_y", color = "log1p(total_counts)") +
  theme_minimal()

print(p)

Note

Here, we're plotting with the color='log1p_total_counts' to visualize the log total transcript counts per cell, but you can replace this with any other variable in your meta dataframe that is the correct dimensions (1xncells) to visualize different aspects of your data.

docs.title: 4. Save the plot as a PNG file
docs.text:
# Save as Plot as PNG
ggplot2::ggsave(
  filename = "cell_xy_log1p_total_counts.png",
  plot     = p,
  width    = 8, height = 8, dpi = 300, units = "in",
  bg       = "white"   
)

⸻

docs.title: Segmenting G4X-data
docs.text:
Here, we lay out a basic approach to resegment your G4X-data. We strongly encourage you to start this process by looking at the existing segmentation using our G4X-viewer. This will allow you to identify where it fails to capture your desired cell morphology.

These instructions are designed to help you take the .jp2 images described in the G4X-data output documentation and run your own segmentation using Cellpose 2. This is typically an iterative process.

docs.title: Basic segmentation approach
docs.text: For this tutorial, we use the most basic Cellpose arguments. It is strongly encouraged that you look into the Cellpose documentation for more advanced options that may suit your needs.

docs.title: 1. Import libraries
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import glymur
from cellpose import models
from cellpose.models import CellposeModel
from skimage.exposure import rescale_intensity

docs.title: 2. Choose which type of segmentation you want to run
docs.text: Nuclear OnlyNuclear +1 markerNuclear +2 markers

docs.title: 3. Load the .jp2 image using glymur
docs.text:
# --- Load JP2 Images ---
nuclear = glymur.Jp2k("path/to/nuclear.jp2")[:]

docs.title: 4. Normalize your nuclear image to the range 0-1
docs.text:
# --- Normalize nuclear image ---
nuclear_norm = rescale_intensity(nuclear, out_range=(0, 1))

docs.title: 5. Run nuclear segmentation
docs.text:
# --- Run nuclear model ---
model = models.CellposeModel(gpu=True, model_type="nuclear")
masks, flows, styles = model.eval(nuclear_norm_subset, channels=[0],
                                    normalize=False)

docs.title: 3. Load the .jp2 images using glymur
docs.text:
# --- Load JP2 Images ---
nuclear = glymur.Jp2k("path/to/nuclear.jp2")[:]
marker1 = glymur.Jp2k("path/to/marker1.jp2")[:]

docs.title: 4. Normalize each image channel to the range 0-1
docs.text:
# --- Normalize each channel separately ---
nuclear_norm = rescale_intensity(nuclear, out_range=(0, 1))
marker1_norm = rescale_intensity(marker1, out_range=(0, 1))

docs.title: 5. Stack your channels for Cellpose input
docs.text:
# --- Stack channels:  marker1_norm = channel 0, nuclear = channel 1 ---
input_img = np.stack([marker1_norm, nuclear_norm], axis=2)

docs.title: 6. Run Cyto3 segmentation
docs.text:
# --- Run Cyto3 ---
model = models.Cellpose(gpu=True, model_type="cyto3")
masks, flows, styles, diams = model.eval(input_img, channels=[1, 0], 
                                            normalize=False)

docs.title: 3. Load the .jp2 images using glymur
docs.text:
# --- Load JP2 Images ---
nuclear = glymur.Jp2k("path/to/nuclear.jp2")[:]
marker1 = glymur.Jp2k("path/to/marker1.jp2")[:]
marker2 = glymur.Jp2k("path/to/marker2.jp2")[:]

docs.title: 4. Normalize each image channel to the range 0-1
docs.text:
# --- Normalize each channel separately ---
nuclear_norm = rescale_intensity(nuclear, out_range=(0, 1))
marker1_norm = rescale_intensity(marker1, out_range=(0, 1))
marker2_norm = rescale_intensity(marker2, out_range=(0, 1))

docs.title: 5. Perform averaging of markers to create a combined membrane channel
docs.text:
Simple AverageWeighted Average 
# combine membrane markers
membrane_combo = (marker1_norm + marker2_norm) / 2  # simple average

# weighted average (sum of weights should be 1)
marker1_weight = 0.35
marker2_weight = 0.65
membrane_combo = ((marker1_weight * marker1_norm) + 
                    (marker2_weight * marker2_norm))

docs.title: 6. Stack your channels for Cellpose input
docs.text:
# --- Stack channels:  membrane = channel 0, nuclear = channel 1 ---
input_img = np.stack([membrane_combo, nuclear_norm], axis=2)

docs.title: 7. Run Cyto3 segmentation
docs.text:
# --- Run Cyto3 ---
model = models.Cellpose(gpu=True, model_type="cyto3")
masks, flows, styles, diams = model.eval(input_img, channels=[1, 0], 
                                            normalize=False)

docs.title: Iterating on your segmentation
docs.text:
After you've generated your segmentation masks, you sould take time to visualize them and determine if they are meeting your needs. This is an iterative process that may take several rounds of tuning.

To save time, you may want to consider using some basic python plotting as well as subsetting your data to speed up iteration. Below are examples of each.

docs.title: Visualize your segmentation
docs.text:
Here is a snippet of code to visualize your segmentation masks overlaid on a single fluorescent image. Notably, the variable this uses are:

  • marker_image: a single fluorescent image (e.g. nuclear or membrane) to show the cell outlines against (same dimensions as masks)
  • masks: the generated segmentation masks from Cellpose
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.figure(figsize=(8,8))

# Show the fluorescent image in blue with a bit of transparency
vmax = np.percentile(marker_image, 99) # remove hot pixels
plt.imshow(
    marker_image, 
    cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=vmax, alpha=0.8, origin="lower"
)

# Draw one contour around each labeled cell
# using half-integer levels to outline integer labels cleanly
levels = np.arange(0.5, masks.max() + 0.5, 1.0)
plt.contour(masks, levels=levels, colors="gray", 
                linewidths=0.7, origin="lower") 

plt.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

docs.title: Subset your images
docs.text:
Since this process can take quite a while on our stitched images, you may want to try to hone your approach first on a smaller, cropped image. For example, after loading your .jp2 image(s), you can subset them with something like this, running your segmentation on that block only:

sz = 1000 # max size of your subset block

# get the image size
x = marker_norm.shape[0]
y = marker_norm.shape[1]

# take the middle 1000 x 1000 pixel block
marker_subset = marker_norm[int((y/2)-int(sz/2)):int((y/2)+int(sz/2)),
                            int((x/2)-int(sz/2)):int((x/2)+int(sz/2))]

docs.title: Applying your segmentation
docs.text: Once you are happy with the outputs, you are ready to save them and run our G4X-helpers tool to regenerate your single cell data using your new segmentation masks.

docs.title: Save your segmentation masks
docs.text:
# ---- Save generated masks ----
np.save("/path/to/output/folder/resegmented_masks.npy", masks)
np.savez_compressed("/path/to/output/folder/resegmented_masks.npz", 
                    nuclei=masks, nuclei_exp=masks)

docs.title: Regenerate your G4X outputs
docs.text:
After you have a segmentation that you are happy with, use the G4X-helpers v4 resegmentation tool to regenerate single-cell data and the G4X-viewer Zarr store for each tissue block. For installation tips, see our guide on installing G4X-helpers. For advanced usage tips, see our resegment documentation.

g4x-helpers resegment /path/to/data/dir/<block_id> \
    --cell-labels /path/to/output/folder/resegmented_masks.npy \
    --branch custom_segmentation

This writes the regenerated outputs to <G4X-DATA>/g4x-helpers/custom_segmentation. Omit --branch to use the default resegment branch. If you use the .npz file saved above, pass --labels-key nuclei_exp to select the mask array.
